title: Popcorn, popped in oil with added butter

content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn is made from corn kernels that explode when heated, creating light, airy pieces. In this version the kernels are popped in vegetable oil and then tossed with butter, giving a rich, buttery flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is one of the oldest snacks, enjoyed by ancient Mexican and Peruvian cultures.
Each kernel contains about 14 % water; when heated the water turns to steam and forces the kernel to pop.
Butter enhances flavor perception by increasing the sensitivity of taste buds to salty and sweet notes.
While popcorn is a staple in movie theaters, the home‑made version lets you control salt and fat levels.
There are over 30 corn varieties suitable for popping; only specific “pop‑corn” types give consistent results.

items.title: Relatively low in calories compared with other snacks
items.content: Popcorn provides about 380 kcal per 100 g, but its low density means you can eat a large volume without excessive calories.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Polysaccharides and polyphenols in corn have antioxidant properties that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Popcorn provides thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Heart‑friendly when prepared with healthy oil
items.content: Moderate consumption of oil‑popped popcorn can help lower LDL cholesterol thanks to its polyunsaturated fat content.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Adding butter raises the calorie count and saturated fat levels; people watching weight or cholesterol should limit portions.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Butter may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with dairy protein intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Burn risk
items.content: Hot popcorn can burn the mouth and esophagus; let it cool slightly before eating.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Excessive salt increases the risk of hypertension; choose a lightly salted version when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Popcorn is perfect as a stand‑alone snack, during movie nights, as a base for sweet or savory mixes, and can be flavored with spices such as paprika, garlic powder, or cheese seasoning.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store popcorn in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator to prevent oil from going rancid. Discard popcorn that becomes soft, develops an off‑odor, or changes color.
